Lecture 15

Complex differentiability and analytic functions

We define the complex derivative and analytic functions and derive the Cauchy–Riemann equations, which are necessary and, with continuous partial derivatives, sufficient. We show that the real and imaginary parts are harmonic when they are C2C^2C2, that their level curves are orthogonal where f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0, and we reconstruct an analytic function from its real part.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Decide whether a function is complex differentiable at a point or analytic on an open set, using the Cauchy–Riemann equations together with a continuity hypothesis.
  • Write the Cauchy–Riemann equations in Cartesian and polar coordinates and compute the derivative from them.
  • Show that the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with C2C^2C2 parts are harmonic, and that their level curves cross at right angles where f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0.
  • Construct a harmonic conjugate on a star-shaped domain, and explain with the heat flow in a cylindrical shell why ln⁡r\ln rlnr has none on an annulus.

Part I differentiated functions of a real variable. Some of them had complex values, such as eλt\ee^{\lambda t}eλt with λ∈C\lambda\in\Cλ∈C, and GM 16 defined their derivative with a real increment of ttt. Part II studies functions of a complex variable zzz, whose derivative uses a complex increment that can approach zero from every direction in the plane. This one requirement implies the Cauchy–Riemann equations for the real and imaginary parts. When these parts are twice continuously differentiable, they are harmonic, like the logarithmic temperature profile in the cylindrical shell of Lecture 2. Branches, integrals, series and residues follow in Lectures 16–21.

15.2 The complex derivative

The derivative of a function of a complex variable is defined by the same difference quotient as for a real variable. The increment hhh is now a complex number.

Definition 15.2 (Complex derivative and analytic function). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open, let f:U→Cf:U\to\Cf:U→C and let z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U. The function fff is complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ if the limit f′(z0)=lim⁡h→0f(z0+h)−f(z0)hf'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}f′(z0​)=h→0lim​hf(z0​+h)−f(z0​)​(15.1) exists, where hhh runs through the nonzero complex numbers with z0+h∈Uz_0+h\in Uz0​+h∈U. The function fff is analytic on UUU if it is complex differentiable at every point of UUU. It is analytic at z0z_0z0​ if it is analytic on some disc Br(z0)B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). An entire function is a function analytic on C\CC.

Many texts say holomorphic for analytic. Lecture 18 shows that a function analytic on UUU is the sum of a convergent power series near each point of UUU, which explains the name.

The limit (15.1) is a limit in the plane. The quotient must approach the same number f′(z0)f'(z_0)f′(z0​) along every line and every curve on which hhh tends to zero.

Since ∣f(z0+h)−f(z0)∣≤∣a∣∣h∣+∣r(h)∣→0,\abs{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}\le\abs a\abs h+\abs{r(h)}\to0,∣f(z0​+h)−f(z0​)∣≤∣a∣∣h∣+∣r(h)∣→0, a function complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ is continuous at z0z_0z0​.

15.3 The Cauchy–Riemann equations

We now express complex differentiability through the partial derivatives uxu_xux​, uyu_yuy​, vxv_xvx​ and vyv_yvy​ of GM 36. Approaching along the two axes gives a necessary condition.

Next let h=ith=\iu th=it with ttt real. Since 1/i=−i1/\iu=-\iu1/i=−i, the difference quotient is f(z0+it)−f(z0)it=v(x0,y0+t)−v(x0,y0)t−i u(x0,y0+t)−u(x0,y0)t.\frac{f(z_0+\iu t)-f(z_0)}{\iu t}=\frac{v(x_0,y_0+t)-v(x_0,y_0)}{t}-\iu\,\frac{u(x_0,y_0+t)-u(x_0,y_0)}{t}.itf(z0​+it)−f(z0​)​=tv(x0​,y0​+t)−v(x0​,y0​)​−itu(x0​,y0​+t)−u(x0​,y0​)​. The full condition involves the derivative of the map F=(u,v)F=(u,v)F=(u,v) of the plane, defined in GM 36 and written DF(x0,y0)DF(x_0,y_0)DF(x0​,y0​) there. GM 36 shows that continuous partial derivatives make a map differentiable. Together with Theorem 15.7 this gives the test used in practice.

Proposition 15.8 (A sufficient condition). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open, and let uuu and vvv be C1C^1C1 on UUU, that is, let their four first partial derivatives exist and be continuous on UUU. If the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at every point of UUU, then f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv is analytic on UUU, and f′=ux+ivxf'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​ is continuous on UUU.

Proof. By the continuity criterion of GM 36, F=(u,v)F=(u,v)F=(u,v) is differentiable at every point of UUU. Theorem 15.7 then shows that fff is complex differentiable at every point, with f′=ux+ivxf'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​ by Proposition 15.6. This function is continuous because its real and imaginary parts are. ■

Example 15.9 (The exponential and the trigonometric functions). We show that ez\ee^zez, cos⁡z\cos zcosz and sin⁡z\sin zsinz are entire and compute their derivatives. These functions are C1C^1C1 on R2\R^2R2, and ux=excos⁡y=vy,uy=−exsin⁡y=−vx.u_x=\ee^x\cos y=v_y,\qquad u_y=-\ee^x\sin y=-v_x .ux​=excosy=vy​,uy​=−exsiny=−vx​. The next two examples show what fails when a hypothesis is dropped.

Example 15.10 (Complex differentiable only on a line). Let f(x+iy)=x2+iy2f(x+\iu y)=x^2+\iu y^2f(x+iy)=x2+iy2 on C\CC. Its parts u=x2u=x^2u=x2 and v=y2v=y^2v=y2 are C1C^1C1, with ux=2x,vy=2y,uy=0=−vx.u_x=2x,\qquad v_y=2y,\qquad u_y=0=-v_x.ux​=2x,vy​=2y,uy​=0=−vx​. Since F=(u,v)F=(u,v)F=(u,v) is differentiable everywhere, Theorem 15.7 shows that fff is complex differentiable exactly on the line y=xy=xy=x. The line contains no disc. Hence fff is analytic at no point. ◃

Example 15.11 (The Cauchy–Riemann equations at a point are not sufficient). Let u(x,y)=∣xy∣u(x,y)=\sqrt{\abs{xy}}u(x,y)=∣xy∣​ and v=0v=0v=0, and let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv. If fff were complex differentiable there, Proposition 15.6 would give f′(0)=ux+ivx=0f'(0)=u_x+\iu v_x=0f′(0)=ux​+ivx​=0. Along the diagonal h=t(1+i)h=t(1+\iu)h=t(1+i) with t>0t>0t>0, however, u(t,t)=tu(t,t)=tu(t,t)=t and f(h)−f(0)h=tt(1+i)=1−i2≠0.\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=\frac{t}{t(1+\iu)}=\frac{1-\iu}{2}\ne0.hf(h)−f(0)​=t(1+i)t​=21−i​=0. Proposition 15.8 does not apply, since ux=12y/xu_x=\tfrac12\sqrt{y/x}ux​=21​y/x​ for x,y>0x,y>0x,y>0 is unbounded near the origin. ◃

15.4 The Cauchy–Riemann equations in polar form

Rotations and radial fields are described more simply in polar coordinates z=reiθz=r\ee^{\iu\theta}z=reiθ with r>0r>0r>0 (GM 15–16). Let UUU be an open set with 0∉U0\notin U0∈/U. For a function uuu on UUU we write u(r,θ)u(r,\theta)u(r,θ) for u(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)u(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)u(rcosθ,rsinθ), keeping the same letter. It is defined for all real θ\thetaθ with reiθ∈Ur\ee^{\iu\theta}\in Ureiθ∈U and is 2π2\pi2π-periodic in θ\thetaθ.

Proposition 15.12 (Polar Cauchy–Riemann equations). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open with 0∉U0\notin U0∈/U, and let uuu and vvv be C1C^1C1 on UUU. At a point z=reiθ∈Uz=r\ee^{\iu\theta}\in Uz=reiθ∈U, the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold if and only if ur=1r vθ,vr=−1r uθ.u_r=\frac1r\,v_\theta,\qquad v_r=-\frac1r\,u_\theta .ur​=r1​vθ​,vr​=−r1​uθ​.(15.7) In that case f′(z)=e−iθ(ur+ivr)f'(z)=\ee^{-\iu\theta}(u_r+\iu v_r)f′(z)=e−iθ(ur​+ivr​).

Proof. By the chain rule of GM 36 for x=rcos⁡θx=r\cos\thetax=rcosθ and y=rsin⁡θy=r\sin\thetay=rsinθ, ur=uxcos⁡θ+uysin⁡θ,uθ=r(−uxsin⁡θ+uycos⁡θ),u_r=u_x\cos\theta+u_y\sin\theta,\qquad u_\theta=r(-u_x\sin\theta+u_y\cos\theta),ur​=ux​cosθ+uy​sinθ,uθ​=r(−ux​sinθ+uy​cosθ), and the same holds for vvv. Write A=ux−vyA=u_x-v_yA=ux​−vy​ and B=uy+vxB=u_y+v_xB=uy​+vx​ for the two Cauchy–Riemann residuals. Substitution gives ur−1r vθ=Acos⁡θ+Bsin⁡θ,vr+1r uθ=Bcos⁡θ−Asin⁡θ.u_r-\frac1r\,v_\theta=A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta,\qquad v_r+\frac1r\,u_\theta=B\cos\theta-A\sin\theta .ur​−r1​vθ​=Acosθ+Bsinθ,vr​+r1​uθ​=Bcosθ−Asinθ. The right-hand sides are the components of (A,B)(A,B)(A,B) after a rotation by the angle −θ-\theta−θ. The squares of the two sides add up to A2+B2A^2+B^2A2+B2, so both vanish exactly when A=B=0A=B=0A=B=0. This proves the equivalence.

Now let the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at zzz. By the continuity criterion of GM 36 the map F=(u,v)F=(u,v)F=(u,v) is differentiable there, so fff is complex differentiable at zzz by Theorem 15.7, with f′(z)=ux+ivxf'(z)=u_x+\iu v_xf′(z)=ux​+ivx​ by Proposition 15.6. Moreover uy+ivy=−vx+iux=i(ux+ivx)u_y+\iu v_y=-v_x+\iu u_x=\iu(u_x+\iu v_x)uy​+ivy​=−vx​+iux​=i(ux​+ivx​). Hence ur+ivr=(ux+ivx)cos⁡θ+(uy+ivy)sin⁡θ=(ux+ivx)(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)=f′(z) eiθ,u_r+\iu v_r=(u_x+\iu v_x)\cos\theta+(u_y+\iu v_y)\sin\theta =(u_x+\iu v_x)(\cos\theta+\iu\sin\theta)=f'(z)\,\ee^{\iu\theta},ur​+ivr​=(ux​+ivx​)cosθ+(uy​+ivy​)sinθ=(ux​+ivx​)(cosθ+isinθ)=f′(z)eiθ, and multiplication by e−iθ\ee^{-\iu\theta}e−iθ gives the formula for f′(z)f'(z)f′(z). ■

Example 15.13 (A logarithm on the cut plane). Let U=C∖(−∞,0]U=\C\setminus(-\infty,0]U=C∖(−∞,0] be the plane cut along the nonpositive real axis. Every z∈Uz\in Uz∈U has exactly one argument in the interval (−π,π)(-\pi,\pi)(−π,π), the principal argument Arg⁡z\Arg zArgz. GM 15 used the same symbol for the argument in [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π). That choice jumps by 2π2\pi2π across the positive real axis, while the argument in (−π,π)(-\pi,\pi)(−π,π) is continuous on UUU, so from now on Arg⁡z\Arg zArgz denotes the principal argument. On UUU it is given by Arg⁡(x+iy)=2arctan⁡yx+x2+y2.\Arg(x+\iu y)=2\arctan\frac{y}{x+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} .Arg(x+iy)=2arctanx+x2+y2​y​.(15.8) Indeed, for θ∈(−π,π)\theta\in(-\pi,\pi)θ∈(−π,π) the half-angle identity gives tan⁡(θ/2)=sin⁡θ/(1+cos⁡θ)=y/(r+x)\tan(\theta/2)=\sin\theta/(1+\cos\theta)=y/(r+x)tan(θ/2)=sinθ/(1+cosθ)=y/(r+x), and θ/2\theta/2θ/2 lies in the range (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2)(−π/2,π/2) of the arctangent. Let u=ln⁡ru=\ln ru=lnr and v=Arg⁡zv=\Arg zv=Argz. In polar form u=ln⁡ru=\ln ru=lnr and v=θv=\thetav=θ for θ∈(−π,π)\theta\in(-\pi,\pi)θ∈(−π,π), so ur=1r=1r vθ,vr=0=−1r uθ.u_r=\frac1r=\frac1r\,v_\theta,\qquad v_r=0=-\frac1r\,u_\theta .ur​=r1​=r1​vθ​,vr​=0=−r1​uθ​. It satisfies eLog⁡z=reiθ=z\ee^{\Log z}=r\ee^{\iu\theta}=zeLogz=reiθ=z, so it inverts the exponential on UUU. Lecture 16 studies this principal logarithm and its other branches. ◃

Arg⁡(x+iy)=2arctan⁡yx+x2+y2.\Arg(x+\iu y)=2\arctan\frac{y}{x+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} .Arg(x+iy)=2arctanx+x2+y2​y​.(15.8)

15.5 Harmonic functions and orthogonal level curves

The Cauchy–Riemann equations couple uuu and vvv. Eliminating one of them gives a single equation for the other.

Definition 15.14 (Harmonic function). Let U⊂R2U\subset\R^2U⊂R2 be open. A real function ψ\psiψ that is C2C^2C2 on UUU is harmonic on UUU if ∇2ψ=ψxx+ψyy=0on U.\laplacian\psi=\psi_{xx}+\psi_{yy}=0\quad\text{on }U.∇2ψ=ψxx​+ψyy​=0on U.(15.9)

This is Laplace’s equation in the plane, with ∇2=∂x2+∂y2\laplacian=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2∇2=∂x2​+∂y2​, the sign used throughout the course. In plane problems, steady temperatures without heat sources and electrostatic potentials without charges are harmonic.

Proposition 15.15 (Harmonic parts). Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic on an open set UUU, and let uuu and vvv be C2C^2C2 on UUU. Then uuu and vvv are harmonic on UUU.

Proof. Differentiate the Cauchy–Riemann equations ux=vyu_x=v_yux​=vy​ and uy=−vxu_y=-v_xuy​=−vx​ with respect to xxx and yyy, respectively: uxx=vyx,uyy=−vxy.u_{xx}=v_{yx},\qquad u_{yy}=-v_{xy}.uxx​=vyx​,uyy​=−vxy​. Here vyxv_{yx}vyx​ denotes (vy)x(v_y)_x(vy​)x​, the derivative first in yyy and then in xxx. By Schwarz’s theorem (GM 37), vxy=vyxv_{xy}=v_{yx}vxy​=vyx​ for a C2C^2C2 function, so uxx+uyy=0u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0uxx​+uyy​=0. In the same way vxx=−uyxv_{xx}=-u_{yx}vxx​=−uyx​ and vyy=uxyv_{yy}=u_{xy}vyy​=uxy​, so vxx+vyy=0v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0vxx​+vyy​=0. ■

Lecture 17 removes the hypothesis that uuu and vvv are C2C^2C2. It shows, with Goursat’s theorem, that the derivative of an analytic function is again analytic, so uuu and vvv have continuous partial derivatives of every order.

Proposition 15.16 (Zero derivative). Let fff be analytic on a domain UUU with f′=0f'=0f′=0 on UUU. Then fff is constant on UUU.

Proof. By Proposition 15.6, f′=ux+ivx=vy−iuyf'=u_x+\iu v_x=v_y-\iu u_yf′=ux​+ivx​=vy​−iuy​. Hence all four partial derivatives vanish on UUU. In particular uuu and vvv are C1C^1C1 with zero gradients. Let z1,z2∈Uz_1,z_2\in Uz1​,z2​∈U, and join them by a polygonal path in UUU. By the gradient endpoint formula of GM 40, u(z2)−u(z1)u(z_2)-u(z_1)u(z2​)−u(z1​) is the integral of ∇u=0\grad u=0∇u=0 along this path, so u(z2)=u(z1)u(z_2)=u(z_1)u(z2​)=u(z1​). The same holds for vvv. ■

The level curves of uuu and vvv are the curves on which uuu or vvv is constant. For a temperature uuu they are the isotherms.

Proposition 15.17 (Orthogonal gradients). Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic on an open set UUU with uuu and vvv of class C1C^1C1, and let z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U with f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0. Then at z0z_0z0​ ∇u⋅∇v=0,∥∇u∥=∥∇v∥=∣f′(z0)∣≠0.\grad u\cdot\grad v=0,\qquad \norm{\grad u}=\norm{\grad v}=\abs{f'(z_0)}\ne0 .∇u⋅∇v=0,∥∇u∥=∥∇v∥=∣f′(z0​)∣=0.(15.10)

Proof. By the Cauchy–Riemann equations, ∇u=(ux,uy)=(ux,−vx)\grad u=(u_x,u_y)=(u_x,-v_x)∇u=(ux​,uy​)=(ux​,−vx​) and ∇v=(vx,vy)=(vx,ux)\grad v=(v_x,v_y)=(v_x,u_x)∇v=(vx​,vy​)=(vx​,ux​). Hence ∇u⋅∇v=uxvx−vxux=0,∥∇u∥2=∥∇v∥2=ux2+vx2=∣f′(z0)∣2.\grad u\cdot\grad v=u_xv_x-v_xu_x=0,\qquad \norm{\grad u}^2=\norm{\grad v}^2=u_x^2+v_x^2=\abs{f'(z_0)}^2 .∇u⋅∇v=ux​vx​−vx​ux​=0,∥∇u∥2=∥∇v∥2=ux2​+vx2​=∣f′(z0​)∣2.■

We now turn to the level sets {z∈U:u(z)=u(z0)},{z∈U:v(z)=v(z0)}.\{z\in U:u(z)=u(z_0)\},\qquad \{z\in U:v(z)=v(z_0)\}.{z∈U:u(z)=u(z0​)},{z∈U:v(z)=v(z0​)}. Since ∇u(z0)≠0\grad u(z_0)\ne0∇u(z0​)=0, one of its partial derivatives is nonzero. The implicit function theorem, which GM 37 cites, applied with that coordinate as the dependent variable, shows that near z0z_0z0​ the level set of uuu is the graph of a C1C^1C1 function, a curve whose normal at z0z_0z0​ is ∇u(z0)\grad u(z_0)∇u(z0​). The same holds for vvv. Hence the two level curves cross at z0z_0z0​ at a right angle.

Let f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0. By Proposition 15.5, a curve through z0z_0z0​ with velocity z′(t0)≠0z'(t_0)\ne0z′(t0​)=0 is mapped by fff to a curve with the nonzero velocity f′(z0)z′(t0)f'(z_0)z'(t_0)f′(z0​)z′(t0​). Every velocity is rotated by the same angle, an argument of f′(z0)f'(z_0)f′(z0​), and stretched by the same factor ∣f′(z0)∣\abs{f'(z_0)}∣f′(z0​)∣. Hence two curves through z0z_0z0​ cross at the same angle as their images. A map with this property is called conformal at z0z_0z0​. With w=f(z)w=f(z)w=f(z), the level curves of uuu and vvv are mapped to the lines Re⁡w=const\Re w=\text{const}Rew=const and Im⁡w=const\Im w=\text{const}Imw=const of the image plane, which cross at a right angle.

Figure 15.1 shows the orthogonal level curves of z2z^2z2 (next example) and of the cylindrical shell of Example 15.22, with aaa, bbb, TaT_aTa​ and c1c_1c1​ defined there.

Example 15.18 (The level curves of z2z^2z2). Let f(z)=z2f(z)=z^2f(z)=z2, with u=x2−y2u=x^2-y^2u=x2−y2, v=2xyv=2xyv=2xy and f′(z)=2zf'(z)=2zf′(z)=2z. Figure 15.1 shows the level curves. Away from the origin u=ku=ku=k and v=kv=kv=k with k≠0k\ne0k=0 are hyperbolas, and each hyperbola of one family crosses each hyperbola of the other at a right angle. At the origin f′(0)=0f'(0)=0f′(0)=0, and the hypothesis of Proposition 15.17 fails. The level set u=0u=0u=0 is the pair of lines y=±xy=\pm xy=±x, the level set v=0v=0v=0 is the pair of axes, and these lines cross at the angle π/4\pi/4π/4. The map z↦z2z\mapsto z^2z↦z2 doubles the angles at the origin, so it is not conformal there. ◃

15.6 Harmonic conjugates

In a plane problem one usually knows a harmonic function, such as a temperature or a potential, and wants the analytic function whose real part it is. Its imaginary part has a name of its own.

Definition 15.19 (Harmonic conjugate). Let uuu be harmonic on an open set U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C. A real function vvv on UUU is a harmonic conjugate of uuu if u+ivu+\iu vu+iv is analytic on UUU.

The word is unrelated to the complex conjugate z‾\conj zz. On a domain a harmonic conjugate is unique up to an additive real constant. Indeed, let v1v_1v1​ and v2v_2v2​ be two of them and w=v1−v2w=v_1-v_2w=v1​−v2​. The difference g=iwg=\iu wg=iw of the two analytic functions is analytic, with real part 000 and imaginary part www. The Cauchy–Riemann equations for ggg give wy=0w_y=0wy​=0 and wx=0w_x=0wx​=0, so g′=iwx=0g'=\iu w_x=0g′=iwx​=0, and ggg is constant by Proposition 15.16.

Existence depends on the shape of the set. As in GM 40, a set UUU is star-shaped about z∗∈Uz_*\in Uz∗​∈U if the segment from z∗z_*z∗​ to every point of UUU lies in UUU. Discs, half-planes and the whole plane are star-shaped about each of their points. The cut plane C∖(−∞,0]\C\setminus(-\infty,0]C∖(−∞,0] is star-shaped about 111, because the segment from 111 to any of its points meets the real axis only in positive numbers.

Theorem 15.20 (Harmonic conjugate on a star-shaped set). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open and star-shaped about z∗∈Uz_*\in Uz∗​∈U, and let uuu be harmonic on UUU. Then uuu has a harmonic conjugate vvv on UUU, and vvv is C2C^2C2. Every other harmonic conjugate is v+cv+cv+c with a real constant ccc.

Proof. Consider the plane vector field F=(F1,F2)=(−uy,ux)\vv F=(F_1,F_2)=(-u_y,u_x)F=(F1​,F2​)=(−uy​,ux​). It is C1C^1C1 on UUU, because uuu is C2C^2C2, and its cross partials agree: ∂xF2−∂yF1=uxx+uyy=0.\partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0 .∂x​F2​−∂y​F1​=uxx​+uyy​=0. By the potential theorem of GM 40 on star-shaped sets, there is a C1C^1C1 function vvv on UUU with ∇v=F\grad v=\vv F∇v=F, that is, vx=−uy,vy=ux.v_x=-u_y,\qquad v_y=u_x .vx​=−uy​,vy​=ux​. These are the Cauchy–Riemann equations. Since uuu and vvv are C1C^1C1, Proposition 15.8 shows that u+ivu+\iu vu+iv is analytic on UUU. The partial derivatives of vvv are C1C^1C1, so vvv is C2C^2C2. A star-shaped set is polygonally connected (GM 40), so UUU is a domain, and uniqueness up to a constant was shown above. ■

In practice we integrate one Cauchy–Riemann equation and fix the remaining function with the other.

Example 15.21 (Reconstructing an analytic function from its real part). Let u(x,y)=e−ycos⁡x+xy((x,y)∈R2).u(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\cos x+xy\qquad\bigl((x,y)\in\R^2\bigr).u(x,y)=e−ycosx+xy((x,y)∈R2). We show that uuu is harmonic, find its harmonic conjugate vvv with v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0, and write f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv as a function of zzz.

First, uuu is C2C^2C2, with uxx=−e−ycos⁡xu_{xx}=-\ee^{-y}\cos xuxx​=−e−ycosx and uyy=e−ycos⁡xu_{yy}=\ee^{-y}\cos xuyy​=e−ycosx. Hence uuu is harmonic on the plane, which is star-shaped, and Theorem 15.20 guarantees a conjugate. The partial derivatives are ux=−e−ysin⁡x+y,uy=−e−ycos⁡x+x.u_x=-\ee^{-y}\sin x+y,\qquad u_y=-\ee^{-y}\cos x+x .ux​=−e−ysinx+y,uy​=−e−ycosx+x. Next, integrate the equation vy=uxv_y=u_xvy​=ux​ with respect to yyy at fixed xxx: v(x,y)=e−ysin⁡x+12y2+g(x),v(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\sin x+\tfrac12y^2+g(x),v(x,y)=e−ysinx+21​y2+g(x), where ggg is a function of xxx alone. The other equation vx=−uyv_x=-u_yvx​=−uy​ requires e−ycos⁡x+g′(x)=e−ycos⁡x−x,\ee^{-y}\cos x+g'(x)=\ee^{-y}\cos x-x,e−ycosx+g′(x)=e−ycosx−x, so g′(x)=−xg'(x)=-xg′(x)=−x and g(x)=−12x2+cg(x)=-\tfrac12x^2+cg(x)=−21​x2+c. The condition v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0 gives c=0c=0c=0. Hence v(x,y)=e−ysin⁡x+12(y2−x2).v(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\sin x+\tfrac12(y^2-x^2).v(x,y)=e−ysinx+21​(y2−x2). Finally we recognize fff. Since eiz=e−y+ix=e−y(cos⁡x+isin⁡x)\ee^{\iu z}=\ee^{-y+\iu x}=\ee^{-y}(\cos x+\iu\sin x)eiz=e−y+ix=e−y(cosx+isinx) and −i2z2=xy+i2(y2−x2)-\tfrac{\iu}{2}z^2=xy+\tfrac{\iu}{2}(y^2-x^2)−2i​z2=xy+2i​(y2−x2), f(z)=u+iv=eiz−i2z2,f′(z)=ieiz−iz.f(z)=u+\iu v=\ee^{\iu z}-\frac{\iu}{2}z^2,\qquad f'(z)=\iu\ee^{\iu z}-\iu z .f(z)=u+iv=eiz−2i​z2,f′(z)=ieiz−iz. As a check, Re⁡f′=−e−ysin⁡x+y=ux\Re f'=-\ee^{-y}\sin x+y=u_xRef′=−e−ysinx+y=ux​, as Proposition 15.6 requires. Every other entire function with real part uuu is f+icf+\iu cf+ic with a real constant ccc. ◃

The plane is star-shaped, so the theorem applies there. On a set with a hole it can fail, and the failure has a physical meaning.

Example 15.22 (Heat flow through a cylindrical shell). In Lecture 2 the steady temperature in the shell a<r<ba<r<ba<r<b, with 0<a<b0<a<b0<a<b, the conductivity κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 and the boundary temperatures Ta≠TbT_a\ne T_bTa​=Tb​, is T=Ta+c1ln⁡ra,c1=Tb−Taln⁡(b/a)≠0.T=T_a+c_1\ln\frac ra,\qquad c_1=\frac{T_b-T_a}{\ln(b/a)}\ne0 .T=Ta​+c1​lnar​,c1​=ln(b/a)Tb​−Ta​​=0. It is harmonic on the annulus A={z∈C:a<∣z∣<b}A=\{z\in\C:a<\abs z<b\}A={z∈C:a<∣z∣<b}. We ask whether it has a harmonic conjugate there, and what such a conjugate would measure.

The conjugate measures the heat flow. Let CCC be a piecewise C1C^1C1 path of GM 40 in the cut annulus, traversed in the direction of increasing parameter. The heat crossing CCC to the right, per unit time and unit length of the cylinder, is therefore ∫j⋅n ⁣ds=−κ∫(Tx ⁣dy−Ty ⁣dx)=−κ∫(Vy ⁣dy+Vx ⁣dx)=−κ (Vend−Vstart),\int\vv j\cdot\vv n\dd s=-\kappa\int(T_x\dd y-T_y\dd x) =-\kappa\int(V_y\dd y+V_x\dd x)=-\kappa\,\bigl(V_{\mathrm{end}}-V_{\mathrm{start}}\bigr),∫j⋅nds=−κ∫(Tx​dy−Ty​dx)=−κ∫(Vy​dy+Vx​dx)=−κ(Vend​−Vstart​), by the Cauchy–Riemann equations and the gradient endpoint formula of GM 40. The field (−Ty,Tx)=c1(−y,x)/r2(-T_y,T_x)=c_1(-y,x)/r^2(−Ty​,Tx​)=c1​(−y,x)/r2 is c1c_1c1​ times the field of GM 40 that has no potential on the punctured plane. Summary

A function is complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ exactly when the map (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) of the plane is differentiable there and its derivative is multiplication by f′(z0)f'(z_0)f′(z0​), which the Cauchy–Riemann equations express. The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with C2C^2C2 parts are harmonic, and on a star-shaped set every harmonic function is such a real part. On an annulus this can fail, as the heat flow through a cylindrical shell shows.

  • Complex derivative: f′(z0)=lim⁡h→0(f(z0+h)−f(z0))/hf'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(z_0+h)-f(z_0))/hf′(z0​)=limh→0​(f(z0​+h)−f(z0​))/h over complex hhh; analytic means complex differentiable on an open set.

  • Cauchy–Riemann: ux=vyu_x=v_yux​=vy​ and uy=−vxu_y=-v_xuy​=−vx​, necessary at a point; sufficient on an open set when uuu and vvv are C1C^1C1; f′=ux+ivxf'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​. In polar form ur=vθ/ru_r=v_\theta/rur​=vθ​/r and vr=−uθ/rv_r=-u_\theta/rvr​=−uθ​/r, with f′=e−iθ(ur+ivr)f'=\ee^{-\iu\theta}(u_r+\iu v_r)f′=e−iθ(ur​+ivr​).

  • Harmonic parts: for analytic fff with C2C^2C2 parts, ∇2u=∇2v=0\laplacian u=\laplacian v=0∇2u=∇2v=0; where f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0 the level curves of uuu and vvv cross at right angles.

  • Harmonic conjugate: exists on a star-shaped set and is unique up to a constant on a domain; ln⁡r\ln rlnr has the conjugate Arg⁡z\Arg zArgz on the cut plane but none on an annulus about 000.

Lecture 16 defines the logarithm and the powers zαz^\alphazα on suitable domains and follows their values along paths that wind around 000.

Stein and R. Shakarchi, Complex Analysis, Chapter 1, §2.2 (holomorphic functions).
